title: Humanoid Robotics

mentor.name: ATLAS-0
mentor.character: Speaks slowly and measures everything. Never lets you move on without a number that backs the posture up.

summary: You will learn why walking on two legs is an unstable problem and how it is solved: centre of mass, support polygon, zero moment point and the divergent component of motion. By the end you can generate a full gait, recover from a push, fall and stand back up, and assemble the whole architecture of a humanoid layer by layer.

lessons.title: The Tall Problem
lessons.goal: Compute how fast a standing humanoid falls once it tilts, and explain why two legs is an unstable problem.
lessons.theory:
A wheeled robot is stable by construction. Turn it off and it stays where it is. A humanoid turned off falls over. That single sentence is the whole difficulty of this course.

The reason is **underactuation**. A humanoid has plenty of motors, but none of them connects to the ground. The only thing between the robot and the world is a foot pressing on the floor, and a foot can push down but never pull up. You cannot command the ground reaction wherever you want it. You can only move your own joints and hope the resulting contact forces keep you up.

The second reason is geometry. Honda ASIMO stands 1.3 m tall with its center of mass around 0.7 m up, resting on feet that are roughly 0.22 m long. That is a tall mass over a short base, an inverted pendulum. Once the pendulum tilts, gravity pulls it further, and the tilt grows exponentially with a time constant `Tc = sqrt(z / g)`, where `z` is the center of mass height. For `z = 0.9 m` that is about 0.30 s. You lose the robot in a fraction of a second, so every controller in this course runs fast and thinks ahead.

- `Tc` is the natural clock of the machine, everything else is measured against it
- taller robot, larger `Tc`, slower fall, which is why big humanoids look calmer than small ones

lessons.title: Counting the Bones
lessons.goal: Build the joint map of a humanoid and count its degrees of freedom by limb.
lessons.theory:
A **degree of freedom** is one independently commanded joint axis. Counting them tells you how much machine you have to control and how much of it you actually need.

The classic layout: 6 per leg, because a leg needs 3 rotations at the hip, 1 at the knee and 2 at the ankle to place the foot anywhere in position and orientation. Then 7 per arm if you want a human style shoulder, elbow and wrist with a redundant elbow swivel, or 6 if you drop it. Then a neck with 2 or 3, a waist with 1 to 3, and hands, which can eat more degrees of freedom than the rest of the body combined.

Real numbers for reference: AIST HRP-2 has 30 degrees of freedom, Boston Dynamics Atlas around 28, Agility Robotics Digit 20, and IIT iCub 53 because most of them are in the hands and face. The trend in commercial humanoids like Unitree G1 or Apptronik Apollo is fewer joints in the legs, more in the hands, since walking is close to solved and grasping is not.

A humanoid is also a **floating base** system. On top of the joints, the pelvis has 6 unactuated degrees of freedom in the world. Those 6 are the ones you fight for the whole course.

lessons.title: Where the Mass Lives
lessons.goal: Compute the whole body center of mass from a list of links with mass and position.
lessons.theory:
The **center of mass**, or CoM, is the mass weighted average of every link position. For a rigid body chain it is `sum(m_i * p_i) / sum(m_i)`. It is the single point that gravity acts on, and almost every balance law in this course is written in terms of it.

Mass in a humanoid is not spread evenly. On a machine like HRP-4, which weighs 39 kg, the torso and pelvis together hold roughly half of it, because that is where the battery, the computers and the heavy hip actuators live. Each leg is around 15 percent, each arm around 5 percent. This is why moving an arm barely moves the CoM while leaning the torso moves it a lot.

Note what the CoM is not. It is not the pelvis, it is not the geometric middle of the robot, and it does not sit at a fixed height. Every time a joint moves, the CoM moves. If your controller assumes the CoM is glued to the pelvis, it will be wrong the moment the robot reaches for something.

lessons.title: The Ground You Own
lessons.goal: Build the support polygon of a standing humanoid from the rectangles of both feet.
lessons.theory:
The **support polygon** is the convex hull of all contact points with the ground, projected onto the floor plane. It is the region where the robot is allowed to push. Outside of it there is nothing to push against.

A flat humanoid foot is a rectangle. HRP-2 uses roughly 0.23 m by 0.13 m. Standing on both feet with a hip width of about 0.18 m, the two rectangles plus the empty space between them form one polygon around 0.23 m by 0.31 m. That gap in the middle counts, because the hull is convex: the robot can put its pressure point between the feet even though there is no material there.

This is the first hard number of the course. Everything about standing still reduces to one question: is the projection of the center of mass inside this polygon. And notice how small it is. Lift one foot and the polygon shrinks to a single rectangle the size of a shoe, which is why single support is where humanoids die.
lessons.task: Return the four corners of each foot rectangle and the axis aligned box that contains both, using the center of mass helper style from the previous lesson.

FOOT_LENGTH = 0.23
FOOT_WIDTH = 0.13
FEET = {
    "left": (0.0, 0.09),
    "right": (0.0, -0.09),
}


def foot_corners(center_xy, length, width):
    cx, cy = center_xy
    hx = length / 2.0
    hy = width / 2.0
    return [
        (cx - hx, cy - hy),
        (cx + hx, cy - hy),
        (cx + hx, cy + hy),
        (cx - hx, cy + hy),
    ]


def support_box(feet):
    points = []
    for center in feet.values():
        points.extend(foot_corners(center, FOOT_LENGTH, FOOT_WIDTH))
    xs = [p[0] for p in points]
    ys = [p[1] for p in points]
    return (min(xs), max(xs), min(ys), max(ys))


print("corners", foot_corners(FEET["left"], FOOT_LENGTH, FOOT_WIDTH))
print("box", tuple(round(v, 4) for v in support_box(FEET)))

lessons.title: Standing Still Is a Decision
lessons.goal: Decide whether a static posture is stable by testing the center of mass projection against the support polygon.
lessons.theory:
**Static equilibrium** has one rule: the vertical projection of the center of mass must fall strictly inside the support polygon. If it does, the robot can hold that posture forever with zero velocity. If it does not, it is already falling and no amount of joint torque will save it without moving a foot.

The useful number is not the yes or no, it is the **stability margin**: the shortest distance from the projected CoM to the boundary. A margin of 0.05 m means you can absorb a small push. A margin of 0.002 m means the robot is technically standing and practically gone, because sensor noise on the CoM estimate of a real humanoid is easily a centimeter.

This is also the definition of the word static. It assumes the robot is not accelerating. The moment the CoM accelerates, this test becomes wrong in both directions: it will reject postures that are fine and accept postures that are not. Fixing that takes the rest of the course.

lessons.title: Frames That Hang Together
lessons.goal: Build a homogeneous transform and compose two of them.
lessons.theory:
Every link of a humanoid carries its own coordinate frame. To know where the right hand is, you chain the transforms from the pelvis outward. A **homogeneous transform** packs a rotation and a translation into one 4 by 4 matrix so that chaining is a single matrix product.

The convention used by nearly every humanoid stack, including ROS 2 and the OpenHRP family, is: x forward, y to the left, z up, right handed. The pelvis frame is the root. A transform `T_a_b` reads as the pose of frame b expressed in frame a, and composing is `T_a_c = T_a_b * T_b_c`. Keep that naming discipline. Half of the bugs in a humanoid are a transform used backwards.

We will write matrices as plain Python lists of lists. Slower than a numeric library, but you see every number, and on a real robot the same math ends up in C anyway.
lessons.task: Write a transform builder for a rotation around z plus a translation, and a 4 by 4 matrix multiply. Compose two links and print the result.
lessons.hint: The rotation block sits in the top left 3 by 3, the translation in the last column, and the bottom row is always 0 0 0 1.

lessons.title: One Leg, Sideways
lessons.goal: Compute forward kinematics of a planar leg with hip, knee and ankle pitch.
lessons.theory:
Start in the **sagittal plane**, the side view. A leg reduced to three pitch joints, hip, knee and ankle, is enough to explain most of walking, because forward motion happens almost entirely in this plane.

Forward kinematics is the easy direction: given joint angles, where is the foot. In the sagittal plane you do not even need matrices. The hip is at height `h`, the thigh has length `l1`, the shin `l2`, and each joint angle adds to the accumulated angle of the segment below it. The ankle position is the sum of two vectors.

Use the sign convention of most humanoid models: a positive pitch angle rotates the segment backwards, so a positive hip pitch swings the thigh back. Get this wrong and your robot walks in reverse, which is a real thing that happens on a first integration day.

lessons.title: Six Ways to Place a Foot
lessons.goal: Extend the leg to the full 6 degree of freedom chain and compute the foot pose in three dimensions.
lessons.theory:
Six is not an arbitrary number. Placing a rigid body anywhere in space takes exactly 6 parameters, 3 for position and 3 for orientation. A leg with 6 joints can therefore put the foot at any reachable pose, and only one set of joint angles gets you there for a given configuration branch.

The standard order from pelvis to foot is hip yaw, hip roll, hip pitch, knee pitch, ankle pitch, ankle roll. HRP-2, HRP-4, TALOS from PAL Robotics and NASA Valkyrie all use this arrangement. Note there is no ankle yaw: you cannot twist the foot against the ground without slipping, so the yaw axis lives at the hip.

Forward kinematics is then a product of 6 transforms plus the fixed link offsets. Slow to write by hand, mechanical to write in code, which is exactly why you write it once as a loop over a joint list.

lessons.title: Nothing Goes All the Way
lessons.goal: Clamp joint commands to their mechanical limits and keep the knee away from full extension.
lessons.theory:
Every joint has a hard limit, and a command that exceeds it does not produce a bigger motion, it produces a fault or a broken gearbox. The controller must clamp before the command leaves the machine, never after.

The knee gets a second, softer limit. At full extension the leg is **singular**: the foot sits at the maximum distance from the hip, and there the Jacobian loses rank, so a small requested foot velocity demands an enormous knee velocity. This is why ASIMO walks with visibly bent knees for its whole life. Modern machines like Cassie and Digit avoid the crouch with a different leg topology, but the singularity is still there, they just plan around it.

A practical rule: keep the knee above 5 to 10 degrees of flexion at all times, and treat any trajectory that asks for less as a planning bug, not as something to clamp silently. Clamping without reporting is how a robot walks wrong for a week before anyone notices.
lessons.task: Write a clamp that respects per joint limits, applies the knee floor, and returns the list of joints that were saturated.
lessons.hint: Raise the lower bound of the knee before clamping, then compare the result against the input to detect saturation.

lessons.title: Solving the Leg Backwards
lessons.goal: Compute analytic inverse kinematics for the leg using the law of cosines on the knee.
lessons.theory:
Walking is planned in terms of foot poses, not joint angles, so you need the inverse: given a desired foot position, find the joints. For a 6 degree of freedom leg with a single knee this has a closed form solution, no iteration and no Jacobian.

The key step is the triangle formed by hip, knee and ankle. Let `d` be the distance from hip to ankle. The law of cosines gives the knee angle directly: `cos(knee) = (l1^2 + l2^2 - d^2) / (2 * l1 * l2)`. If `d` exceeds `l1 + l2` the target is unreachable and the correct response is to report it, not to clamp the cosine and pretend.

Analytic IK is what runs on real machines at 1 kHz. HRP and TALOS both use a closed form leg solver. Iterative solvers appear only for the arms, where redundancy makes a closed form impossible.

import math

THIGH = 0.40
SHIN = 0.38


def knee_from_distance(d):
    if d > THIGH + SHIN or d < abs(THIGH - SHIN):
        return None
    cos_interior = (THIGH * THIGH + SHIN * SHIN - d * d) / (2.0 * THIGH * SHIN)
    cos_interior = min(1.0, max(-1.0, cos_interior))
    interior = math.acos(cos_interior)
    return math.pi - interior


for d in (0.60, 0.75, 0.79):
    k = knee_from_distance(d)
    print(d, None if k is None else round(math.degrees(k), 3))
lessons.hint: The law of cosines gives you the interior angle of the triangle. The knee flexion is pi minus that angle.

lessons.title: Seven Joints, Infinite Elbows
lessons.goal: Compute arm forward kinematics and show the redundancy of the elbow swivel.
lessons.theory:
An arm with 7 joints is redundant: 7 commands for 6 constraints, so an infinite family of postures reaches the same hand pose. The free parameter is the **elbow swivel**, the rotation of the elbow around the line from shoulder to wrist. Your own arm does this. Hold a cup still and move your elbow up and down.

Redundancy is a feature. It lets the robot reach the same object while avoiding a self collision, staying inside joint limits, or keeping the arm out of the camera view. Robonaut 2 and Valkyrie both use 7 degree of freedom arms exactly for this. A 6 joint arm like the one on many industrial machines has no such freedom and hits a wall in cluttered space.

The cost is that inverse kinematics no longer has one answer. You either fix the swivel angle and solve analytically, or you run a numerical solver with a secondary objective. In this course we fix the swivel, which is what most humanoid manipulation stacks do for repeatability.

lessons.solution:
import math

UPPER = 0.30
FORE = 0.26


def wrist_position(shoulder_pitch, elbow):
    a1 = shoulder_pitch
    a2 = shoulder_pitch + elbow
    x = UPPER * math.sin(a1) + FORE * math.sin(a2)
    z = -UPPER * math.cos(a1) - FORE * math.cos(a2)
    return (x, 0.0, z)


def elbow_position(wrist, swivel):
    d = math.dist((0.0, 0.0, 0.0), wrist)
    if d < 1e-9 or d > UPPER + FORE:
        return None
    axis = tuple(c / d for c in wrist)
    along = (UPPER * UPPER - FORE * FORE + d * d) / (2.0 * d)
    radius_sq = UPPER * UPPER - along * along
    radius = math.sqrt(max(0.0, radius_sq))
    helper = (0.0, 1.0, 0.0) if abs(axis[1]) < 0.9 else (1.0, 0.0, 0.0)
    u = (axis[1] * helper[2] - axis[2] * helper[1],
         axis[2] * helper[0] - axis[0] * helper[2],
         axis[0] * helper[1] - axis[1] * helper[0])
    nu = math.dist((0.0, 0.0, 0.0), u)
    u = tuple(c / nu for c in u)
    v = (axis[1] * u[2] - axis[2] * u[1],
         axis[2] * u[0] - axis[0] * u[2],
         axis[0] * u[1] - axis[1] * u[0])
    return tuple(axis[i] * along + radius * (math.cos(swivel) * u[i] + math.sin(swivel) * v[i])
                 for i in range(3))


w = wrist_position(math.radians(30.0), math.radians(60.0))
e0 = elbow_position(w, 0.0)
e1 = elbow_position(w, math.radians(45.0))
print("wrist", tuple(round(v, 4) for v in w))

lessons.title: Mass Through the Chain
lessons.goal: Compute the whole body center of mass by pushing each link mass through forward kinematics.
lessons.theory:
In lesson h0-3 the link positions were handed to you. On a real robot they are not. Each link has a center of mass expressed in its own frame, and you get the world position by running forward kinematics for that link and applying its local offset.

So the whole body CoM is a two step loop: walk the kinematic tree accumulating transforms, and for each link add `mass * (T_link * com_local)` to the running sum. This runs every control cycle, because the CoM moves whenever any joint moves.

Reality check: the CoM you compute is only as good as the mass model. Manufacturers publish inertial parameters that are off by several percent, and cables, covers and batteries are rarely in the model. Identifying the real parameters on the machine, by measuring ground reaction while moving known trajectories, is a standard commissioning step on HRP class robots.

import math

CHAIN = [
    {"name": "pelvis", "angle": 0.0, "offset": (0.0, 0.0), "mass": 9.0, "com_local": (0.0, 0.02)},
    {"name": "torso", "angle": math.radians(10.0), "offset": (0.0, 0.15), "mass": 12.0, "com_local": (0.01, 0.12)},
    {"name": "head", "angle": math.radians(-5.0), "offset": (0.0, 0.30), "mass": 2.0, "com_local": (0.0, 0.08)},
]


def rotate(vec, angle):
    c, s = math.cos(angle), math.sin(angle)
    return (c * vec[0] - s * vec[1], s * vec[0] + c * vec[1])


def chain_com(chain):
    angle = 0.0
    pos = (0.0, 0.0)
    total = 0.0
    acc = [0.0, 0.0]
    for link in chain:
        moved = rotate(link["offset"], angle)
        pos = (pos[0] + moved[0], pos[1] + moved[1])
        angle += link["angle"]
        local = rotate(link["com_local"], angle)
        world = (pos[0] + local[0], pos[1] + local[1])
        total += link["mass"]
        acc[0] += link["mass"] * world[0]
        acc[1] += link["mass"] * world[1]
    return (acc[0] / total, acc[1] / total)


print("com", tuple(round(v, 4) for v in chain_com(CHAIN)))
lessons.hint: Move to the joint first using the previous frame, then apply that joint rotation, then place the local center of mass.

lessons.title: The Base That Floats
lessons.goal: Express the pelvis pose in the world using the IMU orientation and the stance foot as an anchor.
lessons.theory:
Forward kinematics tells you where every link is relative to the pelvis. It says nothing about where the pelvis is in the world, because no joint connects the robot to the ground. That is the **floating base** problem.

The standard trick is to invert the chain. If you assume the stance foot is flat and not slipping, you know its pose in the world, so the pelvis pose is the stance foot pose composed with the inverse of the foot to pelvis transform. Orientation comes from the IMU in the torso or pelvis, which gives roll and pitch absolutely, against gravity, and yaw only by integration, so yaw drifts.

Every humanoid does some version of this, and every one of them has to handle the switch when support changes from one foot to the other. If you recompute the anchor naively at the switch instant, the estimated pelvis jumps by a few millimeters and the controller sees a fake velocity spike. Smoothing that transition is real production work, not a detail.

lessons.title: One Loop for the Whole Body
lessons.goal: Represent the robot as a parent index tree and write a single forward kinematics pass over it.
lessons.theory:
Hand written chains do not scale to 30 joints and two branches. The standard representation is a **kinematic tree** stored as a flat array, where each entry holds its parent index, its joint axis and its fixed offset. Parents always come before children in the array, so a single forward pass computes every link pose with no recursion.

This is exactly how the fast dynamics libraries store a robot, from RBDL to Pinocchio, and it is what the URDF file of any humanoid gets compiled into. The payoff is that adding an arm, a head or a gripper changes data, not code.

Once you have this loop you get the whole body center of mass, every link pose and later the Jacobians from the same structure. Everything above chapter 1 assumes it exists.

import math

TREE = [
    {"name": "pelvis", "parent": -1, "offset": (0.0, 0.0), "angle": 0.0, "mass": 9.0},
    {"name": "torso", "parent": 0, "offset": (0.0, 0.15), "angle": math.radians(8.0), "mass": 12.0},
    {"name": "head", "parent": 1, "offset": (0.0, 0.30), "angle": 0.0, "mass": 2.0},
    {"name": "thigh_r", "parent": 0, "offset": (0.0, -0.05), "angle": math.radians(-20.0), "mass": 3.5},
    {"name": "shin_r", "parent": 3, "offset": (0.0, -0.40), "angle": math.radians(40.0), "mass": 2.0},
]


def rotate(vec, angle):
    c, s = math.cos(angle), math.sin(angle)
    return (c * vec[0] - s * vec[1], s * vec[0] + c * vec[1])


def forward_pass(tree):
    poses = []
    for link in tree:
        parent = link["parent"]
        if parent < 0:
            base_x, base_z, base_a = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0
        else:
            base_x, base_z, base_a = poses[parent]
        moved = rotate(link["offset"], base_a)
        x = base_x + moved[0]
        z = base_z + moved[1]
        poses.append((x, z, base_a + link["angle"]))
    return poses


def body_com(tree, poses):
    total = sum(link["mass"] for link in tree)
    acc_x = sum(link["mass"] * poses[i][0] for i, link in enumerate(tree))
    acc_z = sum(link["mass"] * poses[i][1] for i, link in enumerate(tree))
    return (acc_x / total, acc_z / total)


poses = forward_pass(TREE)
print("head", tuple(round(v, 4) for v in poses[2][:2]))
print("com", tuple(round(v, 4) for v in body_com(TREE, poses)))

lessons.title: What the Floor Pushes Back
lessons.goal: Compute the ground reaction force of a standing humanoid and split it between both feet.
lessons.theory:
Standing still, the floor pushes up with exactly the weight of the robot. For a 45 kg machine that is about 441 N, spread over two feet. Nothing else holds the robot up, so the **ground reaction force**, or GRF, is the only actuation channel that matters for balance.

How it splits between the feet depends on where the center of mass sits. If the CoM is exactly between them, each foot carries half. If it shifts toward the left foot, the left one carries more, in inverse proportion to the distances. This is a lever, so a shift of 4 cm on a 18 cm stance changes the split from 50 50 to about 72 28.

Foot force is measured for real. HRP-2 and TALOS carry six axis force torque sensors in each ankle, and machines like Digit use load cells or estimate the force from joint torques. The vertical component is the first sanity check of any humanoid: if the sum of the two `Fz` readings does not match the weight, either a foot is off the ground or your calibration drifted.

lessons.title: Four Cells Under a Shoe
lessons.goal: Compute the center of pressure of one foot from four load cell readings.
lessons.theory:
Pressure under a foot is not a single point, it is a distribution. The **center of pressure**, or CoP, is the point where the resultant vertical force acts, the pressure weighted average of the contact area.

The cheapest way to measure it is four load cells, one near each corner of the sole. This is what the Nao and many research feet use. The CoP is then the weighted average of the cell positions: `cop_x = sum(f_i * x_i) / sum(f_i)`. If one cell reads zero, that corner is off the ground and the foot is tipping.

In code the deck is a list of dictionaries, one per cell, each with `pos`, the (x, y) position of that corner in the foot frame, and `f`, the force it reads in newtons. Both halves of the average read out of the same entry, so the weight and the position always belong to the same corner.

The CoP has one property that decides everything later: **it can never leave the contact area**. Pressure cannot be negative, because a foot cannot pull the floor. So the CoP is always inside the convex hull of the contact points, by physics, not by choice. Any controller that computes a desired CoP outside the foot is asking for something impossible, and the robot answers by rotating around the foot edge.

lessons.title: Six Axes at the Ankle
lessons.goal: Compute the foot center of pressure from a six axis force torque sensor mounted above the sole.
lessons.theory:
Production humanoids do not use four cells, they use one **six axis force torque sensor** in the ankle. It reports three forces and three moments in its own frame, which sits a few centimeters above the sole.

Getting the CoP from it requires moving the measurement down to the floor. With the sensor at height `h` above the sole, the CoP on the ground is:

- `cop_x = (-m_y - f_x * h) / f_z`
- `cop_y = (m_x - f_y * h) / f_z`

The `f * h` terms are the part people forget, and they matter: a 20 N shear force with a 6 cm offset moves the computed CoP by more than a centimeter, which on a 23 cm foot is a large fraction of your control authority.

Also guard the division. When the foot lifts, `f_z` goes to zero and the CoP becomes meaningless, not infinite. Every real implementation gates this computation on a minimum vertical load, typically 20 to 30 N.

lessons.title: Two Feet, One Point
lessons.goal: Merge the center of pressure of both feet into the global center of pressure.
lessons.theory:
With both feet on the ground you have two local CoPs, one per sole, and one global point that the balance controller cares about. The global CoP is the force weighted average of the two, expressed in the world:

`cop = (fz_left * cop_left + fz_right * cop_right) / (fz_left + fz_right)`

This is why double support is comfortable. The global CoP can sit anywhere on the segment between the two foot CoPs, including the empty air between the feet where no material exists. The support polygon covers that gap and the physics agrees.

Watch the degenerate cases. When one foot unloads, the global CoP must collapse smoothly onto the loaded foot, not jump. Weighting by `fz` does that for free, which is one more reason to use forces rather than a boolean contact flag.

lessons.title: Wrapping the Contacts
lessons.goal: Compute the true convex hull of the contact points instead of the axis aligned box.
lessons.theory:
The box from chapter 0 works only when both feet point forward and sit square. The moment the robot turns a foot, steps onto a ledge or stands with one foot ahead, the real support polygon is the **convex hull** of all contact corners, and the box overestimates it badly.

Overestimating the support polygon is the dangerous direction. It makes the stability test say yes when the robot is already falling. Underestimating only makes you conservative. When in doubt, shrink.

The standard algorithm is Andrew monotone chain: sort the points, then sweep once for the lower hull and once for the upper, dropping any point that makes a non left turn. It is a dozen lines and runs in n log n, which for 8 foot corners is nothing.

lessons.title: How Much Room Is Left
lessons.goal: Compute the signed distance from a point to a convex polygon and use it as the stability margin.
lessons.theory:
Once the support polygon is a real hull, the margin is the shortest distance from the point to any edge. For a convex polygon in counterclockwise order there is a shortcut: for each edge, the signed distance is the cross product of the edge with the vector to the point, divided by the edge length. Inside means positive for every edge, and the margin is the minimum.

This number is what you log, plot and alarm on. A useful set of thresholds for a mid size humanoid: above 0.04 m is comfortable, 0.01 to 0.04 m is working hard, below 0.01 m means the next disturbance takes a step or a fall.

Do not use the margin as the only guard. It measures geometry, not dynamics. A robot with a big margin and a large CoM velocity is in more trouble than one hugging the edge and standing still. Chapter 3 fixes exactly that blindness.

import math

POLY = [(-0.115, -0.155), (0.115, -0.155), (0.115, 0.155), (-0.115, 0.155)]


def signed_margin(point, poly):
    best = None
    n = len(poly)
    for i in range(n):
        a = poly[i]
        b = poly[(i + 1) % n]
        ex = b[0] - a[0]
        ey = b[1] - a[1]
        length = math.hypot(ex, ey)
        if length < 1e-12:
            continue
        distance = (ex * (point[1] - a[1]) - ey * (point[0] - a[0])) / length
        if best is None or distance < best:
            best = distance
    return 0.0 if best is None else best


for p in ((0.0, 0.0), (0.10, 0.14), (0.14, 0.0)):
    print(p, round(signed_margin(p, POLY), 4))

lessons.title: The Point That Rules Them All
lessons.goal: Define the zero moment point and show it coincides with the center of pressure on flat ground.
lessons.theory:
The **zero moment point**, or ZMP, is the point on the ground where the horizontal components of the moment produced by inertia and gravity are zero. Miomir Vukobratovic introduced it in 1968, and it is the concept the entire first generation of walking humanoids, from Honda E series to ASIMO to HRP, was built on.

There is a fact that confuses everyone once and then never again: on flat, unilateral, coplanar contact, the ZMP and the CoP are the same point. The names differ because they come from different sides. The CoP is measured from contact forces. The ZMP is computed from the robot dynamics. When they agree, your model matches reality. When they disagree, something is wrong, and comparing them is one of the best diagnostics on a real machine.

The critical difference is what happens at the boundary. The measured CoP is physically stuck inside the foot. The computed ZMP can come out outside it, and when it does, that is not a contradiction, it is the mathematical signature of a robot that is about to rotate about the foot edge and fall. Some authors call that value the fictitious ZMP or FZMP.

lessons.title: When the Floor Shrinks
lessons.goal: Model the support polygon through a step cycle and measure how much of the time the robot is on one foot.
lessons.theory:
Walking alternates between **double support**, both feet down, and **single support**, one foot down and one in the air. In double support the polygon is roughly 0.23 by 0.31 m. In single support it is one shoe, 0.23 by 0.13 m, an area cut by more than half, and the lateral direction loses almost everything.

The ratio matters. ASIMO and the HRP family spend a long time in double support, often 20 to 30 percent of the cycle, which keeps them stable and makes them look careful. Fast human walking is around 20 percent, running is zero by definition, since both feet leave the ground. Cassie and Digit run gaits with very short double support because their controller does not need the extra polygon.

Every design choice follows from this number. Longer double support means more time with a wide polygon and slower walking. Shorter means faster and more dependent on dynamic balance.

lessons.title: Reaching Past the Edge
lessons.goal: Decide whether a reaching posture stays statically stable, and how far the robot can lean before it must step.
lessons.theory:
This lesson closes the static chapter with the problem that actually shows up on a real machine: the robot reaches forward for an object and quietly falls on its face.

Reaching moves mass. An arm holding a 2 kg tool at 0.6 m in front of a 45 kg robot moves the whole body CoM forward by `2 * 0.6 / 47`, about 0.026 m. That is a quarter of the forward half length of the foot, spent on one light object. Hang a 10 kg crate at that same distance and the shift becomes 0.109 m, which is very nearly the entire foot, so the machine is up on its toes before the arm is even straight. That is the payload this mission carries.

The right move is to check before you plan, not after you move. Compute the CoM of the posture including the payload, evaluate the margin against the polygon, and if the margin is below your threshold, either step forward first or bend the knees and shift the pelvis back. Every capable manipulation stack on a legged robot does this, and it is why Atlas visibly repositions its feet before lifting something heavy.

If you report the last value your loop happened to reach, you are reporting the bound of the loop and not a limit of the robot. The two look identical on screen. A sweep that never sees the margin bind has found no answer at all, and it has to say so out loud rather than hand you back its own upper bound wearing the name of a result.

lessons.title: Newton Owns the Center
lessons.goal: Compute the ground reaction force required for a commanded center of mass acceleration.
lessons.theory:
The whole robot, all 30 joints of it, obeys one equation at the center of mass: `F_grf = m * (a_com + g)`. Nothing else. Every joint torque you will ever command is just a way of producing that force through the contacts.

Read the equation both ways. Forward: if you want the CoM to accelerate forward at 1 m/s2, the ground must push you with a horizontal component of `m * 1`. Backward: given the force the sensors measure, you know the CoM acceleration without differentiating any position twice, which is valuable because differentiating noisy position estimates twice gives garbage.

The vertical component tells you something people miss. To accelerate the CoM upward, the ground must push harder than the weight. A humanoid squatting and standing up quickly can easily see 1.4 times its weight in `Fz`, and the ankle and knee actuators have to be sized for that, not for standing still.
lessons.task: Implement the required ground reaction force for a commanded acceleration and report the load factor relative to standing.
lessons.hint: Gravity adds only to the vertical axis. The horizontal components are mass times acceleration and nothing else.

lessons.title: The Cart on the Table
lessons.goal: Derive the zero moment point from the cart table model and check that it stays inside the foot.
lessons.theory:
The **cart table model** is the simplest picture that gets the ZMP right. Imagine a cart of mass m sliding on a table at constant height z, with the table supported only by the small foot area. Moving the cart shifts the moment about the table edge.

Taking moments about the ground gives the result you used in h2-7, now derived instead of quoted: `p = x - (z / g) * x_ddot`. Accelerate the cart forward and the ZMP moves backwards. That inversion is the heart of walking: to start moving forward, you first push the pressure point behind you, exactly like a person leaning before stepping.

Shuuji Kajita built the classic ZMP preview control on this model, and it is still the reference implementation for HRP class robots. It ignores the arms, the torso rotation and the changing height, and it still walks.

lessons.title: The Linear Inverted Pendulum
lessons.goal: Write the linear inverted pendulum dynamics and integrate it for one second.
lessons.theory:
Constrain the CoM to a horizontal plane of constant height and the inverted pendulum becomes linear:

`x_ddot = (g / z) * (x - p)`

where `p` is the ZMP. That is the **linear inverted pendulum model**, or LIPM, and it is the workhorse of humanoid walking. The constant `omega = sqrt(g / z)` is the natural frequency, the inverse of the time constant from lesson h0-1.

The remarkable part is that the equation is exact under its own assumptions, not a small angle approximation. The price is the constant height constraint, which forbids squatting and stair climbing without corrections, and the assumption that the robot has no angular momentum about the CoM, which forbids the hip strategy of chapter 6.

Even so, this one line has produced more walking robots than any other model in the field.

lessons.title: Closed Form Beats Integration
lessons.goal: Compute the analytic solution of the LIPM and compare it against the numerical integration.
lessons.theory:
The LIPM is linear with constant coefficients, so it has a closed form. With a fixed ZMP at `p`:

- `x(t) = p + (x0 - p) * cosh(w t) + (v0 / w) * sinh(w t)`
- `v(t) = w * (x0 - p) * sinh(w t) + v0 * cosh(w t)`

This matters for three reasons. It is exact, so you can jump to any future time in one evaluation instead of thousands of integration steps. It runs in constant time inside a 1 kHz control loop. And it gives you the structure of the solution, hyperbolic functions, which is where the divergent term of the next lesson comes from.

Use the numerical version as a check, never as the product. If your analytic and numerical answers diverge, one of them has a bug, and finding out which is a five minute job that saves days.

    return (x0, v0)


def numeric(x0, v0, p, t):
    x, v = x0, v0
    for _ in range(int(round(t / DT))):
        v += (G / Z) * (x - p) * DT
        x += v * DT
    return (x, v)

import math

G = 9.81
Z = 0.85
DT = 0.001
W = math.sqrt(G / Z)


def analytic(x0, v0, p, t):
    ch = math.cosh(W * t)
    sh = math.sinh(W * t)
    x = p + (x0 - p) * ch + (v0 / W) * sh
    v = W * (x0 - p) * sh + v0 * ch
    return (x, v)


def numeric(x0, v0, p, t):
    x, v = x0, v0
    for _ in range(int(round(t / DT))):
        v += (G / Z) * (x - p) * DT
        x += v * DT
    return (x, v)


a = analytic(0.02, 0.10, 0.0, 0.6)
n = numeric(0.02, 0.10, 0.0, 0.6)
print("analytic", tuple(round(v, 5) for v in a))
print("gap", round(abs(a[0] - n[0]), 5))

lessons.title: The Energy of Falling
lessons.goal: Compute the orbital energy of the linear inverted pendulum and use it to predict whether the robot crosses over the foot.
lessons.theory:
The LIPM has a conserved quantity, the **orbital energy**:

`E = 0.5 * v^2 - 0.5 * (g / z) * (x - p)^2`

Its sign answers a question you need constantly. If `E` is negative, the CoM does not have enough speed to pass over the support point, so it slows, stops and comes back, like a normal pendulum swing. If `E` is positive, it goes over the top and keeps going. If it is zero you are on the separatrix, the exact boundary.

Kajita used this to plan walking before the capture point formulation existed, and it remains the cheapest way to answer questions such as: with this speed at touchdown, will the robot reach the next step or stall halfway.

lessons.hint: It looks like a mechanical energy with the sign of the potential term flipped, because an inverted pendulum falls away from its equilibrium.

lessons.title: The Part That Runs Away
lessons.goal: Split the pendulum state into its stable and divergent components and compute the divergent component of motion.
lessons.theory:
The hyperbolic solution of h3-4 is a sum of two exponentials, one decaying and one growing. Change coordinates so each has its own variable and the problem becomes trivial. Define the **divergent component of motion**, or DCM:

`xi = x + v / w`

Then `xi_dot = w * (xi - p)`, a first order unstable equation, and `x_dot = -w * (x - xi)`, a first order stable one. The CoM simply chases the DCM and never needs your attention. All you have to control is `xi`.

This is the single most useful change of variables in humanoid walking. It turns a second order unstable system into one unstable scalar per axis. Everything from Johannes Englsberger's DCM control to the walking controllers on TALOS, Valkyrie and most modern research humanoids is built on it. The same quantity, evaluated as `x + v / w`, is also known as the instantaneous capture point.

One caution before you go looking for the convergence on a plot. The CoM chases the DCM, so the gap between the two only closes while the DCM is standing still. Park it by choosing `v = w * (p - x)`, which makes `xi - p` zero and therefore `xi_dot` zero, and the CoM then collapses onto it with time constant `1 / w`, about 0.29 s here. Start both at the same value instead and there is no gap to close at all: the DCM walks away from the pressure point and what you watch growing is the lag of a follower, which is the opposite of what you set out to show.

lessons.title: One Step to Save It
lessons.goal: Compute the instantaneous capture point and the foot placement that stops the robot in a single step.
lessons.theory:
The **capture point** is where you must place the foot to bring the robot to a complete stop in one step. Under the LIPM it is exactly the DCM: `x_cap = x + v / w`.

The reason is the orbital energy of the previous lesson. Put the new support point right at the capture point and the energy becomes exactly zero, so the CoM arrives at the new support with zero velocity and stays. Miss it and you either stall short or keep going.

This gives an operational definition of balance that beats the static polygon test. A humanoid is **1 step capturable** if the capture point lies inside the region it can reach with one step. Jerry Pratt introduced this on the M2V2 robot, and it is the theory behind the step you see Atlas take when someone shoves it. In practice you add a safety shrink, because the model ignores swing time and foot size, and the real capture region is a bit smaller than the ideal one.

Z = 0.85

FOOT_FRONT = 0.115

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Stride
lessons.goal: Define the phases of the gait cycle and locate any time inside the cycle.
lessons.theory:
A **gait cycle** is one full stride, from left heel strike to the next left heel strike. It contains two steps, one per leg. The naming trips people up constantly: a step is half a cycle, a stride is a whole one.

Each leg alternates between **stance**, foot on the ground carrying load, and **swing**, foot in the air moving forward. In human walking, stance is about 60 percent of the cycle and swing 40 percent, and the 10 percent overlap at each end is what produces the two double support phases per cycle.

The phase variable, a number from 0 to 1 within the cycle, is the clock everything else reads. Foot trajectories, ZMP references and gait state machines are all functions of it. Building the robot around a phase variable instead of absolute time is what lets you slow down, speed up or pause a gait without rewriting the trajectories.

lessons.title: Printing Footprints
lessons.goal: Generate a straight line footstep plan with the correct alternating lateral offset.
lessons.theory:
Before any trajectory exists, walking is a list of **footsteps**: where each foot lands, in what order, and when. Everything downstream reads this list.

Two numbers define a straight walk. Step length, the forward distance between consecutive footprints of opposite feet, typically 0.15 to 0.30 m for a mid size humanoid. And step width, the lateral separation, usually equal to the hip width, around 0.18 to 0.22 m. Humans walk with a narrower stance than their hips, but a robot with rigid legs needs the clearance to avoid hitting its own ankle.

The first and last steps are special. The plan starts from the current stance and ends with the feet together, otherwise the robot finishes standing on one leg. Every real planner appends that closing step, and forgetting it is a classic first bug.

lessons.title: Walking Around a Corner

Turning while walking is not a different gait, it is the same footstep list with a heading that changes step by step. Each footprint carries a yaw, and the lateral offset is applied in the rotated frame, not in the world frame.

The limit is the hip yaw joint and the risk of scuffing. A comfortable turn is 10 to 15 degrees per step. Note the asymmetry: turning left is easier on the right foot, since the outer foot travels a longer arc and has more room. Good planners bias the step length per foot during a turn for exactly this reason.

    steps = []
    foot = first

    x, y = 0.0, 0.0
    half = STEP_WIDTH / 2.0
    for _ in range(n_steps):
        yaw += turn
        x += STEP_LENGTH * math.cos(yaw)
        y += STEP_LENGTH * math.sin(yaw)
        side = half if foot == "left" else -half
        fx = x - side * math.sin(yaw)
        fy = y + side * math.cos(yaw)
        steps.append({"foot": foot, "x": fx, "y": fy, "yaw": yaw})
        foot = "right" if foot == "left" else "left"
    side = half if foot == "left" else -half
    steps.append({"foot": foot,
                  "x": x - side * math.sin(yaw),
                  "y": y + side * math.cos(yaw),
                  "yaw": yaw})
    return steps

lessons.title: The Machine That Counts Steps
lessons.goal: Build the gait state machine with double and single support states and explicit transitions.
lessons.theory:
The gait is driven by a **finite state machine** with four states: double support left to right, single support right, double support right to left, single support left. Every module in the stack asks it two questions: which foot is the support, and how far into the current phase are we.

Two transition policies exist and both ship. **Time triggered**, where the state changes when the phase timer expires, is predictable and easy to plan against, which is why the ZMP preview generation of the HRP family uses it. **Event triggered**, where the state changes when the swing foot actually reports contact, is robust on uneven ground, and is what you see on machines walking outdoors.

Production controllers use both: a timer with an early exit on contact and a late exit with a timeout. A pure timer walks off a curb and keeps swinging into thin air. A pure event walks into a hole and waits forever.

lessons.title: The Foot Leaves the Ground
lessons.goal: Generate the horizontal swing foot trajectory with a fifth order polynomial.
lessons.theory:
The swing foot has to travel from the previous footprint to the next one in the single support time, and it must arrive with **zero velocity and zero acceleration**. Anything else lands as an impact, and impacts inject impulses that the balance controller has to absorb after the fact.

The clean way is a fifth order polynomial in the normalized time `s`, from 0 to 1, that satisfies six boundary conditions: position, velocity and acceleration at both ends. The result is the classic quintic profile:

`f(s) = 10 s^3 - 15 s^4 + 6 s^5`

This one function is used everywhere in the course. Multiply it by the total displacement and add the start value and you have a smooth transition for any variable, foot position, pelvis height or arm angle.

lessons.title: Clearing the Ground
lessons.goal: Generate the vertical swing profile with a controlled apex height and flat contact at both ends.
lessons.theory:
The vertical profile is not symmetric with the horizontal one. It has to rise, reach an apex around mid swing, and come back down to exactly zero. A useful shape is two quintics back to back, up to the apex and down again, or a single sine arc if you do not need to place the apex freely.

The apex height is a tuning decision with real consequences. ASIMO lifts about 0.05 m on flat ground. Outdoor machines lift 0.08 to 0.12 m because a stone or a lip of pavement will catch a lower foot. But lifting higher costs knee travel, energy and time, and it moves the leg mass higher, which perturbs the CoM.

Place the apex slightly before mid swing, around `s = 0.45`. The foot then descends more slowly than it rose, which gives the contact detection more time to react before the leg loads.

lessons.title: Landing Without a Bang
lessons.goal: Compute the impact impulse of a touchdown and size the landing velocity that keeps it acceptable.

Touchdown is a collision. The swing leg carries momentum, and the moment the foot meets the floor that momentum has to go somewhere. The impulse is roughly `J = m_eff * v_touchdown`, where the effective mass is somewhere between the leg mass and the whole body mass depending on how stiff the leg is at that instant.

For a 45 kg humanoid, an effective mass of 12 kg landing at 0.3 m/s is 3.6 N s delivered in maybe 20 ms, so an average force of 180 N on top of the body weight. That is the bang you hear when a poorly tuned humanoid walks. It shows up in the force sensors as a spike, in the IMU as a jolt, and in the CoM estimate as a discontinuity.

Three fixes, all used together on real machines: end the vertical trajectory with zero velocity, add compliance at the ankle so the impulse is spread over a longer time, and let the contact detector switch support the instant it sees load rather than waiting for the timer.

lessons.title: Heel, Sole, Toe
lessons.goal: Generate the foot pitch profile for heel strike and toe off, and check the foot does not scuff.
lessons.theory:
A flat foot that stays flat is the simplest gait and the one ASIMO used: the sole lands parallel to the ground and lifts parallel. It works, it is easy on the ZMP, and it limits step length, because the reach of the leg is capped by a fully flat foot.

Human walking rolls: **heel strike** on landing, then the sole flattens, then **toe off** at the end of stance. Rolling extends the effective leg length at both ends of the step, which is why it produces longer strides for the same hip travel. Atlas and several modern humanoids use toe off, and it visibly changes the look of the walk.

The cost is control authority. During heel strike and toe off the contact area collapses to a line, so the support polygon shrinks to almost nothing in the forward direction, and the ZMP has nowhere to move. You buy stride length with stability margin.

There is a second cost, and it is the one that bites in code. Pitching the foot by an angle drops one end of it by `FOOT_HALF * sin(pitch)` below the sole center. Command a flat sole height and the pitched ends go straight through the floor: at 18 degrees of toe off the toe hangs 0.0355 m under the sole, so a sole commanded at 0.03 m is already 0.0055 m into the ground. The height you must command is not the height you want the sole at, it is that height plus the lift the pitch costs you.

lessons.title: One Foot, Full Trajectory

lessons.theory:
This lesson glues chapter 4 together. A swing foot generator takes the start footprint, the target footprint and the phase, and returns a full pose: x, y, z and pitch, plus the velocities that the inverse kinematics and the impact check need.

Three invariants must hold for every sample, and you should assert them, not assume them:

- at `s = 0` the pose sits on the start footprint, touching the floor
- at `s = 1` the pose sits on the target footprint, touching the floor
- the lowest point of the foot never goes below zero during the swing

Violating the third one is the most common gait bug in existence, and it does not look like a bug. It looks like the robot dragging a toe on the ground, losing yaw, and drifting off course over twenty steps.

It has one overwhelmingly common cause, and h4-8 already named it: `swing_z` is the height of the **sole center**, while the invariant is about the **lowest corner**. Feed `swing_z` straight into the pose and at both ends of the swing, where the foot is pitched hardest and `swing_z` is zero, the toe and the heel are hanging below the floor by the full `FOOT_HALF * sin(pitch)`. lessons.title: Drawing the Pressure Path
lessons.goal: Build the zero moment point reference over time from a footstep plan.
lessons.theory:
The footstep list is a set of places. The **ZMP reference** is the continuous path the pressure point must follow through them over time. Producing it is the first job of a walking pattern generator.

The classic reference is piecewise: during single support the ZMP sits at the center of the stance footprint, and during double support it travels from the outgoing footprint to the incoming one. Move it as a straight ramp and you get an acceptable walk. Move it with the quintic from h4-5 and the CoM trajectory that comes out is smoother, because a discontinuous ZMP velocity means a discontinuous CoM jerk.

Two rules that are not optional. The reference must stay inside the current support polygon at every instant, and it must be continuous. A jump in the ZMP reference is a request for an infinite force, and the machine answers with a bang.

lessons.title: Why You Must Look Ahead
lessons.goal: Show that a center of mass trajectory cannot track a zero moment point reference without knowing the future.
lessons.theory:
Here is the counterintuitive fact that defines pattern generation. Under the LIPM the CoM must start moving **before** the ZMP does. To shift the pressure to the next foot, the body has to already be heading that way.

The mathematical reason is the unstable pole. Integrating the LIPM forward from an arbitrary initial state makes the divergent term blow up, so the only bounded solution is the one that integrates the unstable part **backwards from the future**. That is why every pattern generator needs a preview horizon, typically 1.5 to 2 seconds ahead, roughly two steps.

Kajita's 2003 preview control formulated this as an optimal tracking problem with preview gains over the future ZMP reference. The DCM formulation of the next lessons reaches the same answer with less machinery, because it isolates the unstable part explicitly. Either way, the message is identical: no future, no walking.

lessons.title: Planning the End of Every Step
lessons.goal: Compute the divergent component targets at the end of each step by recursing backwards from the final footprint.
lessons.theory:
The DCM formulation solves the future problem with a backward recursion instead of a preview filter. Assume the ZMP is fixed at the support footprint `p_i` during step `i`. Then the DCM at the start of the step relates to the DCM at its end by:

`xi_start = p + (xi_end - p) * exp(-w * T)`

Start from the last step, where the DCM target is simply the final footprint, since the robot must come to rest there. Then walk backwards through the plan, and you get a DCM target at every step boundary in a few lines. No optimization, no matrices.

This is the piece that makes DCM walking so practical. Adding a step is one more recursion term, and replanning mid stride is cheap enough to do at 100 Hz, which is what lets a robot change footsteps in reaction to a push.

Once you have `x` and `xi` you also have the velocity for free, `v = w * (xi - x)`, which is exactly what the whole body controller wants as a reference. No numerical differentiation anywhere in the pipeline.

import math

G = 9.81
Z = 0.85
W = math.sqrt(G / Z)
DT = 0.002


def dcm_at(t):
    return 0.10 * math.exp(0.5 * t) - 0.05


def com_track(duration, x0):

lessons.title: Does the Plan Fit the Feet
lessons.goal: Verify the generated pattern keeps the zero moment point inside the support polygon for the whole horizon.
lessons.theory:
A pattern generator can produce a beautiful trajectory that the feet cannot support. The verification step recomputes the implied ZMP from the generated CoM and checks it against the polygon that is actually available at that instant, single or double support.

Under the DCM formulation the implied ZMP has a shortcut: `p = xi - xi_dot / w`, so no second derivative and no second derivative noise to amplify. That promise holds under two conditions, and both are on you.

The first is that the DCM reference is continuous. Build it the way `dcm_targets` does, backwards from the last footprint, and the value at the end of one step is the value at the start of the next by construction. Restart a fresh exponential from each new footprint instead and the reference jumps at every support switch, which is not a plan any robot could follow.

The second is that you never difference across a support switch. Even with a continuous DCM the implied ZMP is discontinuous there, because it jumps from one foot to the other, so a central difference straddling the switch averages two unrelated regimes and hands you a pressure point metres away. That is not the plan failing, it is your differencing failing, and a check that cannot tell them apart is worse than no check: a single spurious sample will make you refuse a perfectly good gait forever. Difference inside the current phase and the shortcut behaves.

Run this check on every replan, in production, not only in simulation. It costs microseconds and it is the difference between a controller that refuses an impossible step and one that attempts it. Refusing is always available: shorten the step, lengthen the time, or stop.

import math

G = 9.81
Z = 0.85
W = math.sqrt(G / Z)
STEP_TIME = 0.80
DT = 0.01
FOOT_HALF = 0.115
STEPS = [0.0, 0.22, 0.44, 0.44]
PLACED = [0.0, 0.14, 0.28, 0.28]


def dcm_targets(steps, step_time):
    decay = math.exp(-W * step_time)
    targets = [steps[-1]]
    for p in reversed(steps[:-1]):
        targets.insert(0, p + (targets[0] - p) * decay)
    return targets


TARGETS = dcm_targets(STEPS, STEP_TIME)


def phase_of(t):
    return min(int(t // STEP_TIME), len(STEPS) - 1)


def dcm_at(t):
    index = phase_of(t)
    local = t - index * STEP_TIME
    p = STEPS[index]
    return p + (TARGETS[index] - p) * math.exp(W * local)


def dcm_slope(t):
    if phase_of(t - DT) == phase_of(t + DT):
        return (dcm_at(t + DT) - dcm_at(t - DT)) / (2.0 * DT)
    if phase_of(t) == phase_of(t + DT):
        return (dcm_at(t + DT) - dcm_at(t)) / DT
    return (dcm_at(t) - dcm_at(t - DT)) / DT


def implied_zmp(t):
    xi_dot = dcm_slope(t)
    return dcm_at(t) - xi_dot / W


def worst_margin(duration, feet):
    worst = None
    for i in range(1, int(round(duration / DT))):
        t = i * DT
        p = implied_zmp(t)
        center = feet[phase_of(t)]
        margin = FOOT_HALF - abs(p - center)
        if worst is None or margin < worst:
            worst = margin
    return 0.0 if worst is None else worst

placed = worst_margin(2.4, PLACED)
print("worst on the planned feet", round(planned, 4))
print("worst on the feet that landed", round(placed, 4))
print("plan accepted", planned >= 0.0, "/", placed >= 0.0)

lessons.title: Arms Are Not Decoration
lessons.goal: Compute the arm swing that cancels the vertical angular momentum produced by the legs.
lessons.theory:
When the swing leg travels forward it generates angular momentum about the vertical axis. Left uncancelled, that momentum turns the torso, the feet scuff, and the robot yaws off course over a few steps.

The fix is the one your body already uses: swing the opposite arm. The arm produces a counter momentum about the same axis, `L = m * r * v`, and matching it to the leg contribution keeps the net near zero. Human arm swing is not a stylistic habit, it is angular momentum regulation, and studies that strap arms down measure a clear increase in torso rotation and metabolic cost.

The two levers are not the same shape. The arm hangs further from the spine than the leg does, so its radius is the larger of the two, but the leg carries close to three times the mass, and mass wins. The leg contribution is the bigger one, so the arm has to swing faster than the leg to match it, not slower. Check that with the numbers rather than with intuition: if your two products `m * r` come out equal, the answer collapses to the leg speed itself and returning the input unchanged would score exactly the same, which tells you nothing about whether you cancelled anything.

Every credible humanoid does this. ASIMO swings its arms in software with a fixed antiphase gain. Modern whole body controllers derive the arm motion from a centroidal momentum objective instead of a fixed gain, which handles carrying a load in one hand, where the symmetric swing is wrong.

lessons.theory:
The LIPM assumes a constant CoM height. The leg cannot deliver that for free. As the step gets longer, the distance from hip to ankle grows, and to keep the pelvis at the same height the knee has to extend, until it reaches the limit from h1-4 and the constraint breaks.

lessons.title: Ground That Is Not Flat
lessons.goal: Adapt the pattern to a slope and to a stair, moving the reference plane and the foot clearance.
lessons.theory:
On a slope the ZMP still lives on the contact plane, but that plane is tilted. Two changes make the pattern work: express the ZMP reference in the inclined plane, and keep the CoM height measured perpendicular to that plane, since `w = sqrt(g / z)` uses the height above the support, not above sea level.

There is also a friction limit. On a slope of angle `theta` the required tangential force is `m g sin(theta)`, and the available friction is `mu m g cos(theta)`, so the slope is walkable only while `tan(theta) < mu`. With a rubber sole on concrete, `mu` around 0.7, that is roughly 35 degrees in theory and much less in practice, because a foot only needs to slip once.

Stairs are the discrete version. The step height enters the swing profile, the clearance has to exceed the riser plus a margin, and the foot must land fully on the tread, which for a 0.28 m tread and a 0.23 m foot leaves 2.5 cm of error budget at each end. This is why stair climbing demands much better state estimation than flat walking.

lessons.title: Everything the Ankle Can Give
lessons.goal: Compute the maximum ankle torque available from the foot geometry and the recovery it buys.
lessons.theory:
The **ankle strategy** is the first response to a small disturbance: keep the feet where they are and shift the pressure point inside the foot. It is quiet, fast and invisible, and it is what a person does when a bus brakes gently.

Its limit is pure geometry, not motor power. The pressure point cannot leave the sole, so the maximum restoring torque is `tau_max = f_z * d`, where `d` is the distance from the ankle to the foot edge. For a 45 kg robot with the ankle centered on a 0.23 m foot, that is `441 * 0.115`, about 50 N m forward and much less sideways, since the foot is only 0.13 m wide.

Translate that into what it buys you. The maximum CoM acceleration the ankle can command is `a_max = g * d / z`, roughly `9.81 * 0.115 / 0.85 = 1.33 m/s2`. Anything demanding more than that requires the hip or a step, no matter how strong the ankle actuator is. Oversizing the ankle motor does not help. Making the foot longer does.

lessons.title: Throwing the Torso
lessons.goal: Model the hip strategy as an angular momentum exchange and compute the recovery it adds.
lessons.theory:
When the ankle saturates, the next tool is the **hip strategy**: rotate the torso and arms fast in one direction so the reaction accelerates the CoM in the other. It buys real authority without moving a foot, and it is what you see when a person windmills their arms on ice.

It works through the rate of change of angular momentum about the CoM. This is precisely the term the LIPM throws away, which is why the LIPM cannot describe hip recovery.

The catch is that it is a loan, not income. Angular momentum has to come back: the torso has limited travel, so after the recovery the robot must unwind, and the unwinding pushes the CoM the wrong way. The hip strategy handles one impulse, not a sustained force.

The third and strongest strategy is to take a step. Chapter 3 gave the target: place the foot at the capture point `x + v / w`. What chapter 3 did not include is that the step takes time, and during the swing the DCM keeps diverging.

Then check reachability. If the required step exceeds the kinematic limit even with the full swing time, the robot cannot recover with one step, and the honest options are a multi step recovery or a controlled fall. That decision is chapter 8.

lessons.title: Choosing Your Weapon
lessons.goal: Build the strategy selector that picks ankle, hip or step from the measured disturbance.
lessons.theory:
The three strategies form a ladder, and the controller climbs it based on the DCM error, not on the force of the push. Force is a guess. The DCM error is a measurement of the actual state.

A workable policy, with numbers for a mid size humanoid:

- DCM error inside the foot, roughly under 0.06 m: ankle only
- error beyond the foot but recoverable with momentum, up to about 0.12 m: ankle saturated plus hip
- beyond that: step, and pick the target from the previous lesson

The transitions must be continuous. Jumping abruptly from ankle to hip produces a torque discontinuity the machine feels as a knock. Blend by saturating the ankle command first and letting the hip take only what is left over, which is both smoother and easier to debug, since each term stays interpretable.

lessons.goal: Implement the divergent component feedback controller that outputs a commanded zero moment point.

Feedback on the DCM is a one line law with a proven stability condition:

`p_cmd = p_ref + k * (xi_measured - xi_ref)`

with `k > 1`. The condition is not decorative. The DCM error dynamics become `e_dot = w (1 - k) e`, so the error decays only when `k` exceeds 1. A gain of exactly 1 leaves the error frozen, and below 1 the robot diverges while the controller reports that it is working.

Typical values are 1.5 to 3.0. Higher rejects disturbances faster and amplifies estimation noise, and the DCM estimate carries the noise of both the CoM position and its velocity, so it is noisier than either. Around 3.0 most machines start to buzz.

Then clamp the output to the support polygon. The commanded ZMP is a request to the contact, and a request outside the foot is a request the floor will refuse.

lessons.goal: Implement ankle admittance control so the measured center of pressure tracks the commanded one.
lessons.theory:
The balance controller commands a ZMP. The foot has to deliver it, and a position controlled ankle will not, because the real contact depends on the floor, on the sole compliance and on the exact tilt of the foot. The measured CoP will be off by centimeters.

**Admittance control** closes that gap. Measure the CoP with the sensor from h2-3, compare against the command, and move the ankle angle proportionally to the error: `delta_theta = A * (cop_measured - cop_desired)`. The ankle rotates until the pressure lands where it was asked to.

Two production details. The admittance gain must be low, on the order of 0.05 to 0.2 rad per meter of error, because the loop goes through the contact and a high gain oscillates on hard floors. And the ankle offset must be limited and washed out slowly, otherwise the correction accumulates and the foot ends up visibly tilted after a minute of standing.

lessons.title: Level Against Gravity
lessons.goal: Use the inertial measurement unit to keep the pelvis level and reject a tilted floor.
lessons.theory:
The IMU is the only sensor that knows which way is down. The accelerometer gives absolute roll and pitch by measuring the gravity vector, and the gyroscope gives clean angular rate but drifts when integrated. In Python that pitch is `math.atan2(ax, az)`, the two argument arctangent of the standard `math` module, which reads the sign of both components instead of collapsing them into a single ratio, and `math.hypot(ax, az)` from the same module gives the magnitude of that reading. A **complementary filter** takes the low frequency from the accelerometer and the high frequency from the gyroscope:

`angle = a * (angle + gyro * dt) + (1 - a) * angle_from_accel`

with `a` around 0.98 at 500 Hz. It costs three multiplications and it is what runs on a large share of real robots, complex Kalman filters notwithstanding.

Then use it. If the estimated pelvis pitch differs from the reference, correct the hip and ankle pitch to bring it back. This is what keeps the robot upright when it steps on a ramp it did not know about: the trajectory says level, the IMU says tilted, and the difference becomes a joint correction.

One warning that costs people days. The accelerometer measures gravity plus body acceleration, so during a hard push its reading is not vertical. Real filters lower the accelerometer weight when the measured magnitude is far from 9.81.

lessons.title: Guessing Where You Are
lessons.goal: Fuse kinematic odometry with the inertial measurement unit to estimate the center of mass position and velocity.
lessons.theory:
Every controller in this chapter reads the CoM state, and no sensor measures it. It has to be estimated, and the estimate is the weakest link in most humanoid stacks.

Two sources, complementary failure modes. **Kinematic odometry** computes the pelvis from the stance foot as in h1-8, so it is accurate at low frequency and jumps at every support switch. **IMU integration** is smooth and fast but drifts within seconds. Fuse them: use the kinematics for position, the integrated accelerometer for velocity, and let a complementary filter or a small Kalman filter correct the drift. The correction term carries a standard name in estimation, the **innovation**: the measured position minus the predicted one. Scale that innovation by a small gain such as `BETA` and add it to the prediction, and the filter is done.

Velocity is what actually matters, because the DCM is `x + v / w` and `1 / w` is about 0.29 s, so a velocity error of 0.1 m/s is a DCM error of 3 cm, a quarter of the foot. This is why humanoids that balance well have good velocity estimation rather than merely strong actuators.

And handle the support switch explicitly. When the anchor foot changes, the kinematic position jumps. Absorb the jump into an offset that you subtract, so the estimate stays continuous even though the anchor did not.

lessons.title: Standing Up to a Shove
lessons.goal: Integrate estimation, strategy selection and the divergent component controller into a working push recovery loop.
lessons.theory:
This lesson runs the chapter as one loop. At each cycle: estimate the CoM state, compute the DCM, compare against the reference, select a strategy, produce a ZMP command, clamp it to the polygon, and apply it.

Test it the way it gets tested on a real machine. A push is modelled as an instantaneous velocity change at the CoM, `dv = impulse / mass`. A 20 N s impulse on a 45 kg robot is 0.44 m/s, which for `w = 3.4` puts the DCM 0.13 m off, past the foot and into stepping territory.

Be honest about what each rung of that ladder can actually pay for, because the three thresholds and the three capacities are not the same numbers. The ankle is worth `FOOT_HALF`, 0.115 m of pressure point travel. The hip is worth whatever h6-2 measured, `TORSO_INERTIA * MAX_TORSO_ACC / (MASS * G)`, which comes out at 0.049 m of effective shift, so ankle and hip together command 0.164 m. At the gain of h6-5 the controller asks for `GAIN * error`, so that authority covers a divergent component error of 0.164 / 2.2, about 0.074 m. The `HIP_LIMIT` of h6-4 is 0.12, which is a nameplate written in error units at unity gain, not a promise that the hip can serve an error of 0.12 at a gain of 2.2. Escalate on the capacity and you never command pressure the foot cannot provide; escalate on the nameplate and there is a band of pushes where the selector says hip while the ankle is already saturated and the robot is quietly leaving.

So the loop needs all three rungs, and the top one has to move a foot. Reporting `step` and then not stepping is the worst of both: the selector is right, the machine is not, and the peak error it prints is the distance it travelled while nothing happened. When you do step, propagate with h6-3, `xi_td = p + (xi - p) * exp(w * T_swing)`, and be careful which `p` you hand it. During the swing the ankle and the torso are both saturated holding the fall back, so the pressure point is at the edge of the authority, not at the centre of the foot. Predict with the centre and you will aim the foot far beyond where the DCM actually arrives, land long, and have to step back.

What you should see: small pushes absorbed by the ankle with the ZMP moving inside the foot and returning, medium pushes handed to the torso, and large pushes putting a foot down and ending standing. If your loop reports ankle recovery for a 0.44 m/s push, the clamp is missing and the controller is commanding pressure outside the foot, which reality will not provide.

lessons.title: The Space You Can Touch
lessons.goal: Compute the reachable workspace of an arm and test whether a target is inside it.
lessons.theory:
The **workspace** of an arm is the set of points the wrist can reach. For a two link arm it is the annulus between `|l1 - l2|` and `l1 + l2` around the shoulder, intersected with the joint limits, which usually cut away a large part of it.

Numbers for a mid size humanoid: upper arm 0.30 m, forearm 0.26 m, so the outer radius is 0.56 m and the inner one 0.04 m. But the reach that matters is the one relative to the feet, not the shoulder, because reaching demands balance, which chapter 2 already showed. The useful workspace of a standing humanoid is much smaller than its geometric workspace.

Never plan into the boundary. Near full extension the arm is singular exactly like the knee in h1-4, so a small hand motion needs a huge joint speed. Keep a margin of a few centimetres and treat targets in that band as reachable only after taking a step. The inner boundary has the same problem for the same reason: an arm folded right up against `|l1 - l2|` is just as singular as one stretched straight, and a target that close needs the shoulder moved, not the elbow bent further.

A word on testing this. Three classes need three targets that actually land in three classes, and a target sitting exactly on a band edge is not one of them: whichever way the comparison happens to be written decides its class, so the test tells you about your `<=` and nothing about the arm. Place the fixtures inside the bands, not on the seams.

lessons.title: Two Hands, One Object
lessons.goal: Enforce the closed chain constraint of carrying a rigid object with both hands.
lessons.theory:
The moment both hands hold the same rigid object, the arms are no longer independent. They form a **closed kinematic chain**, and the relative pose between the two hands must stay exactly constant. Violate it by a millimeter and the arms fight each other through the object, building up internal forces that show up as motor heat and, with a stiff object, as a broken wrist.

The clean formulation is to command the object pose and derive both hand poses from it: `T_hand_left = T_object * T_grasp_left`. The grasp transforms are captured once at the moment of grasping and then held fixed. Never command the two hands from separate trajectories.

The constraint is worth checking rather than trusting, and checking it means sweeping the yaw, not printing the distance at two poses. Every derivation agrees at yaw zero, including the wrong ones, so two samples that match prove nothing at all. Rotate through a full turn and a derivation that forgot to rotate one of the grasps gives itself away immediately, with the hands closing to nothing at half a turn.

This is how bimanual manipulation works on Toyota T-HR3, on Valkyrie and on any robot that carries a box. The internal force that remains, the squeeze holding the object, is controlled separately and deliberately, which is the subject of the grasp lessons.

lessons.title: Picking How to Hold It

lessons.theory:
Grasps are not interchangeable. The taxonomy that most stacks use collapses to three practical families. A **power grasp** wraps the whole hand around the object and carries the most load with the least precision. A **precision grasp** uses fingertips, carries little and places accurately. A **pinch** is the two finger version for thin objects.

The selection rule is mostly geometry and mass. Above roughly 1 kg or 60 mm of width, a power grasp. Under 30 mm and light, a pinch. In between, precision.

Each family carries its own payload limit, and the selector is what protects it. Nothing heavier than 1 kg ever reaches a precision grasp, so that family cannot be handed more than the 1 kg it holds. The pinch has no such protection, because a thin object can still be dense, and neither has the power grasp once the object is heavier than the arm was built for. Printing the limit next to the type is what makes those two cases visible before the hand closes.

The reason this matters on a humanoid rather than an arm on a table is that grasp choice changes the load path all the way to the feet. A power grasp on a heavy object lets you keep the elbow close to the body, which keeps the payload near the CoM and preserves the stability margin of h2-9. A precision grasp at full extension does the opposite.

lessons.title: Will It Slip
lessons.goal: Compute the required grip force from the friction cone and the object weight.
lessons.theory:
A grasp holds because friction resists the tangential load. With two opposing fingertips and a friction coefficient `mu`, the grip force needed to hold a weight is `f_grip >= m * g / (2 * mu)`.

Put numbers on it. A 1 kg object with rubber on plastic, `mu` around 0.6, needs `9.81 / 1.2`, about 8.2 N of squeeze. Now accelerate the hand upward at 3 m/s2 and the required force rises by a third. Real controllers apply a safety factor of 1.5 to 2 over the computed minimum, and they raise the grip when the wrist force sensor sees the object load increase. Squeezing harder than needed is not free either: it deforms soft objects and it heats the finger motors, which on small hands is a real thermal limit.

The detector is a strict inequality against the edge of the friction cone, so a test that feeds it a load sitting exactly on that edge tells you nothing about slipping and everything about which way you wrote the comparison. The head is a two or three joint pointing mechanism, and aiming it is straightforward trigonometry: transform the target into the neck frame, then `pan = atan2(y, x)` and `tilt = atan2(-z, sqrt(x^2 + y^2))`.

What is not straightforward is that the head is mounted on a moving body. A humanoid walking bobs vertically by a centimeter or two and pitches with every step, so a head commanded in body coordinates points somewhere different at every instant. Every gaze command must be computed in world coordinates and converted through the current body pose, every cycle.

Gaze also has a social function. iCub, Pepper and most robots meant to work near people follow a rule: look at what you are about to do. Turning the head toward the object before the arm moves tells a person what is coming, and it is one of the cheapest safety features available, because a predictable robot is a safe robot.

import math

NECK = (0.0, 0.0, 1.42)
PAN_LIMIT = math.radians(80.0)
TILT_LIMIT = math.radians(45.0)


def gaze_angles(target, body_yaw=0.0):
    dx = target[0] - NECK[0]
    dy = target[1] - NECK[1]
    dz = target[2] - NECK[2]
    c, s = math.cos(-body_yaw), math.sin(-body_yaw)
    lx = c * dx - s * dy
    ly = s * dx + c * dy
    pan = math.atan2(ly, lx)
    tilt = math.atan2(-dz, math.hypot(lx, ly))
    pan = min(PAN_LIMIT, max(-PAN_LIMIT, pan))
    tilt = min(TILT_LIMIT, max(-TILT_LIMIT, tilt))
    return (pan, tilt)

A camera on a walking robot shakes. Every step pitches the torso and the image smears, which destroys feature tracking exactly when the robot needs it most.

Biology solved this with the **vestibulo ocular reflex**: the inner ear measures head rotation and the eyes counter rotate with a latency of about 10 ms, far faster than visual tracking could ever be. Robots copy it directly. Read the gyroscope, command the neck to rotate the opposite way, and do it in the fastest loop you have, ahead of any vision processing.

The key insight is that this is **feedforward**, not feedback. You are not waiting to see blur and then correcting, you are cancelling a measured rotation before it reaches the image. Feedback on the image is always too late, since a camera at 30 Hz cannot fix a disturbance at 5 Hz. Every humanoid that does useful vision while walking has some version of this loop.
